about.visionText: To become one of the leading contracting and engineering companies in Sudan and the region, by delivering sustainable projects, maintaining the highest execution standards, and earning client trust through excellence at every project stage.

sudanSchoolsReport.metaTitle: The Cost of Rehabilitating Government Schools in Sudan | MS Square Engineering
sudanSchoolsReport.metaDescription: A data-driven look at what it really costs to rehabilitate a Sudanese government school in 2026 — from $15,000 light repairs to $900,000 full reconstructions, based on real Khartoum market prices.
sudanSchoolsReport.heading: The Cost of Rehabilitating Government Schools in Sudan
sudanSchoolsReport.subheading: A Practical Reading of the Contracting Market
sudanSchoolsReport.excerpt1: There is no single "damaged Sudanese school." Real cost per school ranges from USD 15,000 for a light repair of a small school to USD 900,000 for the full reconstruction of a large educational complex — and that wide spread is exactly what produces the "astronomical" figures seen in the media, figures that collapse into rational numbers once each school is classified by its actual condition.
sudanSchoolsReport.excerpt2: This report is built on real 2026 market prices in Khartoum and on documented, executed projects — not press statements. For any organisation or investor planning to fund school rehabilitation in Sudan, it lays out a practical cost model: a four-tier damage classification, current material and per-square-metre prices, and the exchange-rate discipline needed to keep any dollar-denominated contract accurate.

stats.label: Children out of education in Sudan

sudanSchoolsReport.figureTitle: Estimated Rehabilitation Cost by School Category (USD)
sudanSchoolsReport.figureNote: Figure 6 — MS Square practical cost bands, based on 2026 Khartoum market prices and documented project data.
sudanSchoolsReport.keyTakeawaysTitle: Why the Numbers Vary So Much
keyTakeaways: Damage is not uniform: from light surface damage to full destruction by direct shelling — four distinct condition tiers drive four very different budgets.
The gap between the official and parallel exchange rate can radically change a contract's dollar value depending on which rate is used.
Core material prices — cement and steel especially — jumped sharply within just a few months in 2026 due to transport disruption and FX volatility.
Around 80% of existing school buildings were built by community initiative without engineering supervision, so their baseline condition varies widely.
sudanSchoolsReport.ctaText: Complete material and cost-per-square-metre tables, documented project benchmarks, market sources, and our field-survey methodology — in the full report.
sudanSchoolsReport.ctaNote: PDF · English · Research & Cost Advisory Division
sudanSchoolsReport.sourceNote: Based on Khartoum construction-market prices (mid-2026), UNICEF and UNESCO/GPE reporting, and documented rehabilitation projects in Sudan and South Sudan. Full source list in the report.

electricalWiringReport.metaTitle: Why Electrical Wiring Should Be a Priority in School Rehabilitation | MS Square Engineering
electricalWiringReport.metaDescription: Why rehabilitating a Sudanese primary school should upgrade the electrical installation, not just repaint it — circuit coordination, protection, earthing, fire-rated cable and IEC standards explained.
electricalWiringReport.heading: Why Electrical Wiring Should Be a Priority in the Rehabilitation of Sudanese Primary Schools
electricalWiringReport.intro: Rehabilitation is an opportunity to replace unsafe, inefficient and outdated systems with solutions that provide a safer, more reliable and more sustainable environment for students and staff — and this is particularly important when it comes to electrical installations.
electricalWiringReport.s1Title: Rehabilitation Should Not Mean Rebuilding the Same Problems
electricalWiringReport.s1Text1: When a school is rehabilitated, the objective should not simply be to restore the building to the condition it was in before deterioration.
electricalWiringReport.s1Text2: In many existing schools, electrical systems have evolved through years of modifications, extensions and repairs. Circuits may have been extended without proper load assessment, cables may have deteriorated, protective devices may no longer correspond to the actual loads, and electrical connections may have been exposed to moisture, mechanical damage or excessive heating.
electricalWiringReport.s1Text3: Simply repainting walls, repairing ceilings and replacing doors while leaving the original electrical installation substantially unchanged may therefore restore the appearance of a school without addressing one of its most important safety systems.
electricalWiringReport.s1CalloutTitle: Improve it, don't just preserve it
electricalWiringReport.s1CalloutText: A rehabilitation project should improve the electrical installation, not merely preserve it.
electricalWiringReport.s2Title: Why Electrical Systems Deserve Special Attention in Schools
electricalWiringReport.s2Text1: Schools are not ordinary buildings. They contain large numbers of children, many of whom have limited awareness of electrical hazards. Classrooms, offices, laboratories, workshops, stores and sanitary facilities may all have different electrical requirements.
electricalWiringReport.s2Text2: At the same time, school buildings are often occupied for long periods and may contain combustible materials such as books, paper, furniture and teaching materials.
electricalWiringReport.s2Text3: An electrical fault that might be manageable in a small residential building can therefore have much more serious consequences in a school.
risks: Unprotected cables exposed to mechanical damage.
Excessive use of extension cables and multiple adaptors.
electricalWiringReport.s2Closing: The objective of rehabilitation should be to reduce these risks systematically.
electricalWiringReport.s3Title: The Cable Is Not the Only Issue
electricalWiringReport.s3Text1: A common misconception in rehabilitation projects is that installing a “better cable” automatically makes the electrical installation safer. It does not.
electricalWiringReport.s3Text2: The safety of an electrical circuit depends on the coordination between the conductor, the load, the installation method and the protective device.
electricalWiringReport.s3Text3: IEC 60364-4-43 specifically addresses protection against overcurrent and the coordination between conductors and protective devices. In practical terms, the circuit breaker must protect the conductor under the actual installation conditions.
electricalWiringReport.designFactorsLabel: This means that selecting a cable should never be based only on its nominal cross-sectional area. The design should consider:
electricalWiringReport.s3RightQuestion: “Which cable and protection system are appropriate for the intended load and installation conditions?”
electricalWiringReport.s4Intro: For an existing primary school, the electrical system should be assessed circuit by circuit before any replacement decision is made. The assessment should normally include:
electricalWiringReport.s4dbIntro: The distribution board should be inspected for:
electricalWiringReport.s4dbNote: Where appropriate, old or inadequate distribution boards should be replaced rather than repeatedly repaired.
electricalWiringReport.s4lightText1: Lighting circuits should be separated from socket and high-load circuits.
electricalWiringReport.s4lightText2: For typical lighting circuits, 1.5 mm² copper conductors may be appropriate in many installations, but the final conductor size must be determined from the design current, installation method, voltage drop and protective device. The important principle is that the cable size should be calculated rather than selected simply because it is commonly used.
electricalWiringReport.s4socketText1: Socket circuits generally require more capacity than lighting circuits. A 2.5 mm² copper conductor is commonly used for socket final circuits, subject to the actual design and installation conditions.
electricalWiringReport.s4socketText2: In a school, socket circuits should receive particular attention because users may connect fans, computers, printers, chargers and other appliances.
electricalWiringReport.s4socketText3: Where required, socket circuits should be protected by residual-current protection. This can significantly reduce the risk of electric shock from faults involving exposed conductive parts.
electricalWiringReport.s4socketText4: IEC 60364-4-41 establishes requirements for protection against electric shock in low-voltage installations.
electricalWiringReport.s5Title: Air Conditioners and High-Load Equipment Require Separate Design
electricalWiringReport.s5Text1: Another common rehabilitation mistake is to treat every electrical point as if it has the same load. It does not.
electricalWiringReport.s5Text2: An air conditioner, water pump, photocopier or workshop appliance can impose a substantially higher load than a lighting point.
electricalWiringReport.s5Text3: Dedicated circuits should therefore be provided where required, with conductor sizes and protective devices selected according to the actual equipment rating and operating conditions.
electricalWiringReport.s5Text4: For example, a 4 mm² or 6 mm² conductor might be appropriate for a particular air-conditioning circuit, but it would be technically incorrect to specify one size universally without knowing the equipment capacity, supply arrangement, cable length, installation method and voltage-drop requirements. That distinction is important in professional rehabilitation work.
electricalWiringReport.s6Text1: Cable selection also matters from a fire-safety perspective. Modern cable standards distinguish between normal electrical performance and behaviour under fire.
electricalWiringReport.s6Text2: IEC 60332 addresses flame propagation tests, while IEC 60331 concerns circuit integrity under fire conditions. These are not interchangeable requirements.
electricalWiringReport.s6Text3: A flame-retardant cable is intended to limit flame propagation. A fire-resistant cable, by contrast, is designed to maintain circuit integrity for a specified period under fire conditions. This distinction matters.
electricalWiringReport.s6Text4: A school does not necessarily require fire-resistant cables for every ordinary lighting and socket circuit. Fire-resistant cables are generally associated with circuits that must continue operating during a fire, such as designated emergency systems.

fireCards.title: Flame-Retardant
fireCards.text: Limits how far flame propagates along the cable run — the baseline expectation for ordinary lighting and socket circuits.

fireCards.title: Fire-Resistant
fireCards.text: Maintains circuit integrity for a specified period under fire — reserved for circuits that must keep operating during a fire, such as emergency systems.

fireCards.title: Low-Smoke Zero-Halogen (LSZH)
fireCards.text: Reduces smoke and corrosive gases, improving evacuation conditions in occupied public buildings such as schools.

electricalWiringReport.s6Text5: For occupied public buildings such as schools, low-smoke and low-halogen cable technologies can provide additional safety benefits where specified by the project design and applicable standards — reducing smoke and corrosive gases can improve conditions during evacuation.
electricalWiringReport.s6Text6: The specification should therefore clearly state the required cable performance instead of simply saying “good quality cable.”
electricalWiringReport.s7Text1: Where the existing installation contains deteriorated, undersized or unsuitable conductors, replacing them with properly specified copper conductors can provide a significant improvement in reliability.
electricalWiringReport.s7Text2: The conductor cross-sectional area should be selected through electrical design rather than by visual comparison with the existing cable. For building installations, conductor specifications and resistance characteristics are addressed by IEC 60228, while cable construction requirements are covered by relevant cable standards such as IEC 60502 for applicable cable types.
electricalWiringReport.s7Closing: The cheapest cable is rarely the cheapest solution over the life of a building.
electricalWiringReport.s8Title: Connections Are Often More Important Than the Cable
electricalWiringReport.s8Text1: A high-quality cable can still become a fire hazard if it is badly connected.
electricalWiringReport.s8Text2: Poor terminals, loose screws, inadequate crimping, damaged insulation and uncontrolled cable joints can create localized resistance.
electricalWiringReport.s8Text3: Localized resistance generates heat. Repeated heating can deteriorate insulation, which can eventually lead to arcing, short circuits or fire.
electricalWiringReport.connectionItemsLabel: Rehabilitation should therefore include inspection and replacement of:
electricalWiringReport.s8Closing: Where possible, joints should be contained within appropriate accessible enclosures and installed according to the applicable wiring standard.
electricalWiringReport.s9Text1: Replacing cables without correcting the earthing system is incomplete rehabilitation.
electricalWiringReport.s9Text2: The protective earthing system provides a controlled path for fault current and supports the operation of protective devices. The rehabilitation assessment should therefore verify:
earthingChecklist: Effectiveness of protection against electric shock.
electricalWiringReport.s9Text3: Testing should be performed after installation rather than assuming that a visually correct installation is electrically safe.
electricalWiringReport.s9Text4: IEC 60364-6 establishes requirements for verification and testing of low-voltage electrical installations.
electricalWiringReport.s10Title: The Rehabilitation Should End With Testing — Not Painting
electricalWiringReport.s10Text1: A technically complete rehabilitation does not finish when the last cable is installed. It finishes after the installation has been inspected and tested.
electricalWiringReport.s10Text2: Depending on the installation, testing should include appropriate verification such as:
testingChecklist: Earth-fault loop / protective measures as applicable.
Visual inspection of cable routes and terminations.
electricalWiringReport.s10Text4: The results should be documented as part of the project handover. This creates an important distinction between:
electricalWiringReport.s10After: “Electrical installation verified and safe for operation”
electricalWiringReport.s11Title: A Practical Rehabilitation Specification for a Typical Classroom
electricalWiringReport.s11Intro: A typical classroom should not simply receive “new wiring.” The scope should be developed based on the actual building and loads, but may include:

classroomCircuits.title: Lighting
classroomCircuits.note: New or upgraded circuit, correctly sized conductors, efficient LED luminaires.

classroomCircuits.title: General Power
classroomCircuits.note: Dedicated socket circuits with residual-current protection where required.

classroomCircuits.title: High-Load Equipment
classroomCircuits.note: Dedicated circuits for air conditioners and other significant loads.

lightingScope: New lighting circuit where existing wiring is inadequate.
highLoadScope: Dedicated circuits for air conditioners or other significant loads.
protectionScope: Surge protection where justified by the electrical design and supply conditions.
electricalWiringReport.s12Title: The Cost Question: What Does Better Electrical Rehabilitation Actually Cost?
electricalWiringReport.s12Text1: This is where rehabilitation decisions must become quantitative. Using the exchange-rate assumption provided for this article:
electricalWiringReport.exchangeFormula: Cost in SDG = Cost in USD × 5,700
electricalWiringReport.s12Text2: However, the exchange rate alone does not determine the local cost of an electrical installation.
electricalWiringReport.s12Text3: The final cost also depends on:
electricalWiringReport.s12Text4: For this reason, a professional BoQ should not publish a generic “price per metre” without a current supplier quotation. For example, if the approved 2.5 mm² copper cable is quoted locally at X SDG per conductor metre, and a classroom requires Y metres of conductor, then:
electricalWiringReport.s12Formula2: Total conductor length ≈ 3 × route length (phase + neutral + protective conductor)
electricalWiringReport.s12Text5: This is why the phrase “the classroom needs 100 metres of cable” is technically incomplete — one must specify whether this means 100 metres of cable route or 100 metres of individual conductors, before allowing for vertical drops, distribution-board connections and reasonable installation wastage.
electricalWiringReport.s13Title: The Better Way to Compare Rehabilitation Costs

optionA.title: Minimal Repair
points: Reuse most existing wiring and replace only visibly damaged sections.
Old cable sections remain in service.
Hidden joints and unknown conductor capacity.

optionB.title: Proper Electrical Rehabilitation
points: Replace deficient circuits and upgrade protection.
Higher initial cost, but a significantly safer, more maintainable installation.

electricalWiringReport.s13Closing: Option A will almost always appear cheaper at the quotation stage. But the purpose of rehabilitation is not to minimize today’s invoice — it is to improve the condition and performance of the asset for the years ahead.
electricalWiringReport.s14Title: Rehabilitation Is an Opportunity, Not Just a Repair
electricalWiringReport.s14Text1: When a school is already being rehabilitated, walls may already be opened, conduits may already be accessible, ceilings may already be removed, and contractors are already mobilized. That creates an opportunity.
electricalWiringReport.s14Text2: Replacing a deficient electrical installation during rehabilitation is usually far more practical than attempting to correct the same installation after the building has been fully finished.
electricalWiringReport.s14PrincipleText: If we are going to rehabilitate a school, we should not simply restore the old system. We should use the rehabilitation process to correct known deficiencies and deliver a safer, more reliable and more sustainable electrical installation.
electricalWiringReport.s14Text3: For primary schools, this is not simply an engineering upgrade. It is a safety intervention.
electricalWiringReport.s14Text4: Children should not inherit the electrical problems created by decades of deferred maintenance. They should inherit a school that has been rehabilitated properly.
electricalWiringReport.s15Text1: At MS Square Engineering, we believe rehabilitation should begin with assessment rather than assumptions. Our approach is based on:
electricalWiringReport.s15Text2: For electrical rehabilitation, this means assessing the existing installation, identifying unsafe or deficient components, designing the required upgrades, preparing a detailed Bill of Quantities, executing the work according to the approved specification, and testing the completed installation before handover — because rehabilitation is not simply about making a building look new. It is about making the building perform better than it did before.
